authoredPrompt: This figure is an oblique three-dimensional drawing of a disk drive, rendered as line art with gray shading and five callout labels. Two circular platters are stacked one above the other, each a flat gray disk with visible edge thickness; a leader from the upper left points to the top disk and reads "platter." A dark vertical rod runs through the centers of both disks and protrudes above and below the stack, tagged "spindle" by an arrow at the top. A long curved arrow sweeping across the top surface toward the upper right gives the direction in which the platters turn. Drawn concentrically on the top platter, partway between the spindle and the rim, is a heavy gray circle labeled "track." A small solid black tip resting on that circle is labeled "read/write head"; it sits at the end of a slender tapered arm that extends to the right and broadens into a rounded pad. A second arm of identical shape reaches the lower platter, and the two pads are joined by a short vertical post serving as their shared pivot, with two leaders below marked "arms." A double-headed arrow beside the head shows the arm swinging toward and away from the spindle. Separating the spin of the platters from the radial swing of the arms makes plain how any point of a magnetized surface is brought under a head. The drawing lays out the mechanical parts of the storage device and fixes the names used for them.
authoredInteractions:
- Slider for sweeping the arm angle from outer rim toward the spindle; the read/write head moves across concentric tracks while the platter stays in place, showing how seeking selects a radius before rotation brings sectors under the head.
- Animation for platter spin with the selected track highlighted; the head remains stationary while marks on the disk pass beneath it, clarifying the split between rotational motion and radial head positioning.
authoredContext:
Figure 18.2 shows a typical disk drive. The drive consists of one or more platters, which rotate at a constant speed around a common spindle. A magnetizable material covers the surface of each platter. The drive reads and writes each platter by a head at the end of an arm. The arms can move their heads toward or away from the spindle. When a given head is stationary, the surface that passes underneath it is called a track. Multiple platters increase only the disk drive’s capacity
and not its performance.
